subject: Dividing a frequency list into bands

messages.author: e1b933a0d5bbe14f
messages.subject: Dividing a frequency list into bands
parts:
Need a little hand with something. I'm trying to divide a word frequency list into frequency bands. So all the first 1000 words will be assigned a 1, the second a 2, etc. I could simply make a vector with a thousand 1s, then a thousand 2s, etc, but this ignores the issue of ties, which becomes an issue lower down the list. I'm defining a frequency band as x (here x=1000) words plus all the ties of the last frequency count, so in a large corpus, a frequency band (especially in the lower ranks) might actually consist of a few thousand items.

For the sake of illustration/reproducible data, suppose we have the first two columns of the data below. We want to divide it into bands of 5, or more in the case of ties. The third column is what we want to generate. 

Any suggestions?

WORD FREQ BAND
A 3000 1
B 2500 1
C 2300 1
D 2200 1
E 2100 1
F 2000 2
G 2000 2
H 1800 2
I 1800 2
J 1800 2
K 1600 3
L 1600 3
M 1500 3
N 1500 3
O 1400 3
P 1400 3
Q 1300 4
R 1200 4
S 1000 4
T 900 4
U 800 4
V 800 4
W 800 4
X 700 5
Y 500 5
Z 500 5

messages.author: e1b933a0d5bbe14f
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Dividing a frequency list into bands
parts:
Not a stupid question. It's difficult to explain.

I want the bins to be of x length. In the real data I'm working with, this means each bin would include, in theory, 1000 words each. Bin #1 has the 1000 most frequent words, Bin #2 has the next 1000, etc. So sort(table(data),decreasing=T)[1:1000] would be one way of showing the first bin.

But...

Suppose you look carefully at the data and you see that the item at position 1000 and the one at 1001 are actually the same frequency. I don't want to split them up just because one is later in alphabetical order or otherwise arbitrarily sorted. So in this case, I would want the first bin to have 1001 items (and the next bin the next 1000, assuming no tie at the 2000th position).

In the sample data I gave, I want to split the data into bins containing 5 elements. The first five lines go into the first bin, and the second five go into the second bin. No problems there. However, for the third frequency band, the fifth (overall 15th) element has the same frequency as the sixth (Words 'O' and 'P' both have frequencies of 1400.). Rather than splitting them up, we put them in the same bin, so this bin has six items. Bin 4 has a similar issue: a three-way tie at the cutoff point, so this one actually gets seven items. (Bin 5 has three leftovers, which, given Zipf's Law, is not realistic, but I ran out of letters.)

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Dividing a frequency list into bands
parts:
Ok, I now understand what kind of output you want, but I am not sure
- how straightforward it is to decide automatically what frequencies
to group together - would 3001 still be in the same bin as 3000, 2500,
etc.? would 4000? would 10000?
- whether it is the best approach to bin data that we know are Zipfian
into bins with large equal numbers.

Esp. given the second point, I would probably just go with cut(FREQ, 5):

table(cut(FREQ, 5))
# (498,1e+03] (1e+03,1.5e+03] (1.5e+03,2e+03] (2e+03,2.5e+03]
(2.5e+03,3e+03]
# 8 6 7 4
1

But maybe I'm missing something here ... Let's see what others say

messages.author: 97ce067823027f53
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Dividing a frequency list into bands
parts:
To address the original question, you can construct the frequency bands "manually" with a while-loop with condition that the remaining (sorted) word list is not empty, with an inner while-loop for the current bin where you keep adding items until both of the things are true: you have collected at least binMax items in the current bin, and the current word is not tied with the previous word. Inside the inner while-loop, remove words from the remaining word list as they are added to the bin. After breaking out of the inner while-loop (inside the main while-loop), you increment the bin number.



I can't think of an easier way like using some fancy indexing trick in R to break ties for you and construct the bands.

But I think Stefan's point is the heart of it. It reminds me of a talk he gave way back in 2008 (maybe?) on automatically detecting an 'optimal' or 'best' way to group years for historical corpus data. It's much like the frequency bands here. Why 1000? Might there be a data-driven way to automatically detect bins?

Very much pseudocode, but should be standard.
I can't think of an easier way like using some fancy indexing trick in R to break ties for you and construct the bands.

But I think Stefan's point is the heart of it. It reminds me of a talk he gave way back in 2008 (maybe?) on automatically detecting an 'optimal' or 'best' way to group years for historical corpus data. It's much like the frequency bands here. So I don't have a good answer for either # bins or deciding which bin a word should go into. I guess these questions might be aided by considering overall research question.

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Dividing a frequency list into bands
parts:
I know too little about this kind of stuff but I am always wondering
whether nice bands of 1000 are really theoretically that well
motivated. But even then: creating bands of 1000 in R is easy, but
then that's not what you want anyway, right? Because in your first
data set, you did _not_ have bins of that width, but also wanted bin
size to play a role. Binning automatically by 1000s is easy, but the
additional criterion will require a user-defined weighting of what to
do when the two criteria conflict. In your example, _you_ decided that
bin 2 is _not_ 1000-2000 so that would be much harder to implement
especially since it's not obvious that all such conflicts of criteria
should be resolved in the same way.

messages.author: 8dafe35eb614235f
messages.subject: Re: Dividing a frequency list into bands
parts:
It's not pretty, but I think the following does what Kevin originally asked about, although I couldn't figure out how to deal with the last row of the data frame:
library(dplyr)


df <- data.frame(
  word = c("hola", "hello", "goodbye", "chao", "something", "here", "whatever", "it", "may", "be"),
  freq = c(92, 81, 81, 63, 43, 12, 23, 43, 45, 56)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(freq))


band_width <- 2
all_band <- rep(NA, nrow(df))
cur_band <- 1
counter <- 0
for (i in 1:nrow(df)) {
  counter <- counter + 1
  if (counter >= band_width & (df[i, 'freq'] != df[i + 1, 'freq'])) {
    all_band[i] <- cur_band
    cur_band <- cur_band + 1
    counter <- 0
  } else {
    all_band[i] <- cur_band
  }
}


print(data.frame(df, all_band))



One way to do what Alex mentioned with a "data-driven way to automatically detect bins" might be to use kmeans(). Note that the group labels are not ordered by frequency ranges, as they are simply unique numbers that serve as labels.
library(dplyr)


num_word <- 100
band_width <- 10
df <- data.frame(
  word = replicate(num_word, paste(sample(letters, 5), collapse = "")),
  freq = sample(seq(1, 10000), num_word, replace = T)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(freq))


group <- kmeans(df$freq, 10)
print(data.frame(df, group$cluster))
print(data.frame(group$center, group$size))



To do a non-equi join, along the lines of what Stefan said about using cut():
library("dplyr")

df <- data.frame(
  word = c("hola", "hello", "goodbye", "chao", "something", "here", "whatever", "it", "may", "be"),
  freq = c(92, 81, 81, 63, 43, 12, 23, 43, 45, 56)
) %>%
  arrange(freq)

cut_offs <- data.frame(
  threshold = seq(from = 90, to = 0, by = -10),
  bin = LETTERS[10:1]
)

df %>%
  mutate(band = cut(df$freq, c(cut_offs$threshold, 100), labels = cut_offs$bin)) %>% print()


or with data.table:
library("data.table")
library("dplyr")

df <- data.table(
  word = c("hola", "hello", "goodbye", "chao", "something", "here", "whatever", "it", "may", "be"),
  freq = c(92, 81, 81, 63, 43, 12, 23, 43, 45, 56)
) %>%
  arrange(freq)
setkey(df, freq)

cut_offs <- data.table(
  threshold = seq(from = 90, to = 0, by = -10),
  bin = LETTERS[1:10]
)
setkey(cut_offs, threshold)

cut_offs[df, roll = Inf] %>%
  select(word, freq = threshold, bin) %>%
  arrange(desc(freq))

Sorry, I e-mailed my reply a bit earlier instead of posting it here, so here it goes again.


If I understand correctly, you want to bin your frequencies so that you get 5 UNIQUE frequencies per bin. If this is so, I think your second bin should go from F all the way down to, and including, P (observations 6 to 16), and you'll only get 4 rather than 5 bins. Here's my try:

Assuming your data is in a data frame called data:

x <- 5 # bin length
unique_freq <- unique(data$FREQ) # unique freq values
bins <- ceiling(length(unique_freq) / x) # number of bins
binned <- rep(1:bins, each = x)[seq_along(unique_freq)] # bin unique freqs
counts <- table(data$FREQ)[as.character(unique_freq)] # how many times each
binned <- rep(binned, counts)
data$BIN <- binned
